question: A 64-year-old man presents with acute-onset right-sided hemiparesis and expressive language deficits. Physical examination reveals intact speech comprehension, but his speech is non-fluent, effortful, and telegraphic. He cannot repeat phrases accurately. Which of the following cortical structures is most likely damaged in this patient?

options.text: Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Postcentral gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Angular gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Middle frontal gyrus of the non-dominant hemisphere

explanation:
The patient exhibits Broca aphasia (expressive, motor aphasia characterized by non-fluent speech, preserved comprehension, and impaired repetition). Broca area is located in the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus (specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis, Brodmann areas 44 and 45) in the dominant (usually left) cerebral hemisphere.

Distractor rationales:
- Superior temporal gyrus contains Wernicke area; damage causes fluent, nonsensical aphasia with impaired comprehension.
- Postcentral gyrus contains the primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann 3, 1, 2); damage causes contralateral somatosensory loss.
- Angular gyrus lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation).
- Middle frontal gyrus contains the frontal eye fields (Brodmann 8).

question: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her family because she fails to dress the left side of her body, bumps into doorframes on her left, and denies that her left arm belongs to her. Neurological exam reveals normal visual acuity, but she ignores visual, auditory, and tactile stimuli on her left side. An MRI is ordered. In which of the following lobes is a lesion most likely to be found?

options.text: Non-dominant parietal lobe
Dominant parietal lobe
Non-dominant temporal lobe
Dominant frontal lobe
Non-dominant occipital lobe

explanation:
This patient exhibits hemispatial neglect syndrome (asomatognosia, anosognosia, and unilateral spatial inattention). Hemispatial neglect is classic for lesions of the non-dominant (typically right) parietal cortex (specifically the inferior parietal lobule/temporoparietal junction). The right hemisphere mediates spatial attention across both the right and left hemispaces, whereas the left hemisphere only attends to the right hemispace; thus, non-dominant parietal damage severely compromises contralateral (left) spatial awareness.

Distractor rationales:
- Dominant parietal lobe lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome or apraxia.
- Non-dominant temporal lobe damage can impair visuospatial memory or facial recognition (prosopagnosia) when fusiform gyrus is involved.
- Dominant frontal lobe damage leads to Broca aphasia and executive dysfunction.
- Non-dominant occipital lobe lesions result in contralateral homonymous hemianopia without multimodal neglect.

question: A 72-year-old male with long-standing hypertension suffers an acute ischemic stroke. On exam, he presents with complete paralysis of the left face, left arm, and left leg, but has no sensory loss, visual field defect, or aphasia. CT angiogram reveals occlusion of a penetrating branch of the middle cerebral artery. The lesion is located in which anatomical division of the internal capsule?

options.text: Posterior limb
Anterior limb
Genu
Retrolenticular limb
Sublenticular limb

explanation:
The patient presents with a classic pure motor lacunar stroke (hemiparesis affecting face, arm, and leg equally without cortical signs). The descending corticospinal motor fibers are densely packed in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, supplied by lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery. Lacunar infarction due to lipohyalinosis or microatheroma at this location produces contralateral pure motor hemiparesis.

Distractor rationales:
- Anterior limb carries frontopontine and anterior thalamocortical fibers; lesions cause executive or behavioral changes.
- Genu contains corticobulbar fibers projecting to cranial nerve motor nuclei; isolated genu lesions cause pure dysarthria-facial paresis without dense hemiplegia.
- Retrolenticular limb carries optic radiations (visual fibers from LGN to visual cortex).
- Sublenticular limb carries auditory radiations from MGN to primary auditory cortex.

question: During a neurosurgical approach to the pineal region and quadrigeminal plate, the surgeon identifies a cranial nerve that emerges from the posterior (dorsal) surface of the brainstem and decussates before exiting. Which cranial nerve is being identified?

options.text: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Abducens nerve (CN VI)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

explanation:
The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique among all cranial nerves in two major anatomical respects: it is the ONLY cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal (posterior) aspect of the brainstem (just inferior to the inferior colliculi of the midbrain tectum), and its fibers completely decussate before emerging, innervating the contralateral superior oblique muscle. It also has the longest intracranial course and is most susceptible to trauma.

Distractor rationales:
- Oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges ventrally from the interpeduncular fossa of the midbrain.
- Abducens nerve (CN VI) emerges ventrally at the pontomedullary junction near the midline pyramids.
- Trigeminal nerve (CN V) emerges from the mid-ventrolateral pons.
- Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges ventrally between the pyramid and the olive in the pre-olivary sulcus of the medulla.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with persistent hoarseness, dysphagia, and loss of the gag reflex on the left. On physical examination, when she says 'ah,' her uvula deviates to the right. MRI demonstrates a mass lesion compressing the post-olivary sulcus of the rostral medulla. Which set of cranial nerves emerges from this specific sulcus?

options.text: CN IX, CN X, and CN XI
CN VI, CN VII, and CN VIII
CN III and CN IV
CN V alone
CN XII alone

explanation:
The post-olivary (retro-olivary or posterolateral) sulcus of the medulla oblongata is the exit site for cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XI (cranial accessory). Lesions in this groove compromise ipsilateral pharyngeal and laryngeal elevation, sensation, and vocal cord function, leading to dysphagia, hoarseness, absent gag reflex, and deviation of the uvula away from the affected side.

Distractor rationales:
- CN VI, VII, and VIII emerge from the cerebellopontine angle / pontomedullary junction.
- CN III emerges from the interpeduncular fossa; CN IV emerges dorsally.
- CN V emerges from the anterolateral pons.
- CN XII emerges from the pre-olivary sulcus (between pyramid and olive).

question: A 67-year-old man has a sudden onset of right-sided visual field deficit. Visual field confrontation testing confirms a right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Brain MRI demonstrates an infarction localized to the calcarine sulcus banks. Which cerebral artery is occluded, and which cortical area does it supply?

options.text: Posterior cerebral artery supplying Brodmann area 17
Middle cerebral artery supplying Brodmann area 4
Anterior cerebral artery supplying Brodmann area 6
Middle cerebral artery supplying Brodmann area 22
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplying Brodmann area 39

explanation:
The primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17, striate cortex) lines the superior and inferior banks of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe. It is primarily supplied by cortical branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). PCA occlusion leads to contralateral homonymous hemianopia. The macular region (located at the occipital pole) often receives dual collateral blood supply from middle cerebral artery branches, resulting in the classic finding of macular sparing.

Distractor rationales:
- MCA supplies Brodmann 4 (primary motor cortex) over the lateral convexity.
- ACA supplies Brodmann 6 (premotor and supplementary motor cortex) on the medial frontal surface.
- MCA supplies Brodmann 22 (superior temporal gyrus/Wernicke area).
- PICA supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum, not cerebral Brodmann areas.

question: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after suddenly speaking fluent, grammatically complex sentences that make no sense ('word salad'). She cannot follow verbal commands and is unable to repeat phrases, but she appears unbothered and unaware of her communication deficit. The lesion is located in which cortical structure?

options.text: Posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere
Inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere
Arcuate fasciculus alone
Cingulate gyrus in the non-dominant hemisphere
Parahippocampal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere

explanation:
This patient has Wernicke aphasia (receptive/sensory aphasia: fluent, paraphasic speech with neologisms, impaired auditory comprehension, and impaired repetition). Patients typically exhibit anosognosia (unawareness of their deficit). Wernicke area corresponds to Brodmann area 22 and is located in the posterior aspect of the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere.

Distractor rationales:
- Inferior frontal gyrus houses Broca area; lesions cause non-fluent expressive aphasia.
- Conduction aphasia from isolated arcuate fasciculus damage causes fluent speech with preserved comprehension, but severely impaired repetition.
- Cingulate gyrus is part of the limbic system; damage causes apathy or akinetic mutism.
- Parahippocampal gyrus mediates episodic memory encoding and spatial memory.

question: A 52-year-old accountant presents following a stroke. Testing reveals that he can no longer perform simple addition or subtraction (acalculia), cannot write his signature (agraphia), cannot distinguish his ring finger from his index finger (finger agnosia), and confuses his left hand with his right hand. His speech and comprehension are otherwise normal. Damage to which cortical area accounts for this clinical tetrad?

options.text: Dominant angular gyrus
Dominant inferior temporal gyrus
Non-dominant supramarginal gyrus
Dominant precentral gyrus
Non-dominant orbitofrontal cortex

explanation:
The classic tetrad of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation is diagnostic of Gerstmann syndrome. This syndrome is caused by a lesion in the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobule, often due to an embolic stroke in the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery.

Distractor rationales:
- Inferior temporal gyrus is involved in visual object processing (ventral stream).
- Non-dominant supramarginal gyrus lesions impair spatial perception and can contribute to neglect or constructional apraxia.
- Precentral gyrus is the primary motor strip.
- Orbitofrontal lesions result in disinhibition and altered personality.

question: An 80-year-old man presents with an acute right hemispheric stroke. On neurological examination, his eyes are conjugate and involuntarily deviated toward the right side. However, he can successfully track moving objects across the midline when his head is turned passively (intact doll's-eye reflex). Which cortical center is involved in this gaze deviation?

options.text: Right frontal eye field in the middle frontal gyrus
Left frontal eye field in the inferior frontal gyrus
Right paramedian pontine reticular formation
Left abducens nucleus
Bilateral superior colliculi

explanation:
The frontal eye field (FEF, Brodmann area 8) is located in the posterior portion of the middle frontal gyrus. Each FEF projects across the midline to the contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) to generate voluntary conjugate saccadic eye movements to the opposite side. An acute destructive cortical lesion of the right FEF eliminates the drive to look left, resulting in tonic conjugate deviation toward the side of the lesion ('looking toward the lesion'). The brainstem gaze centers are intact, preserving oculocephalic reflexes.

Distractor rationales:
- Left FEF damage would cause gaze deviation to the left.
- PPRF lesions cause conjugate gaze deviation away from the side of the lesion ('looking toward the hemiparesis').
- Abducens nucleus damage causes ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy plus impaired contralateral medial rectus adduction on conjugate gaze (lateral gaze palsy).
- Superior colliculi mediate reflexive vertical gaze and pupillary reflexes.

question: A 63-year-old woman suffers an ischemic stroke resulting from occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery (ACA). Based on the somatotopic organization of the motor homunculus, which of the following clinical deficits will be most pronounced on physical examination?

options.text: Left lower extremity weakness greater than upper extremity weakness
Left face and arm weakness greater than lower extremity weakness
Right lower extremity weakness alone
Bilateral upper extremity weakness
Isolated left facial palsy with sparing of the forehead

explanation:
The motor homunculus along the precentral gyrus is somatotopically organized: the lower extremity and genitalia are represented on the medial surface of the hemisphere (paracentral lobule), which is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery (ACA). The trunk, upper extremity, and face are represented along the lateral convexity of the hemisphere, which is supplied by the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Therefore, an ACA infarction classically causes contralateral lower extremity motor and sensory loss that is significantly more severe than upper extremity involvement.

Distractor rationales:
- Contralateral face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness is characteristic of an MCA stroke.
- Right ACA stroke causes left-sided (contralateral) deficits, not right-sided.
- Bilateral upper extremity weakness suggests central cord syndrome or bilateral watershed infarcts ('man-in-a-barrel').
- Isolated facial palsy without limb weakness suggests a peripheral CN VII lesion or isolated cortical branch infarct.

question: A 42-year-old man who survived herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) encephalitis is brought to clinic by his sister. She notes that he has become inappropriately placid, continually puts non-food objects like pencils and coins into his mouth, exhibits hypersexual behavior toward strangers, and cannot recognize previously familiar objects despite normal visual acuity. Brain MRI demonstrates bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis in the anterior temporal lobes. This constellation of findings is best described as which of the following?

options.text: Klüver-Bucy syndrome
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Anton-Babinski syndrome
Capgras syndrome
Fregoli delusion

explanation:
This clinical picture (hyperorality, hypersexuality, docility/loss of fear, and visual agnosia) is classic for Klüver-Bucy syndrome, caused by bilateral lesions of the anterior temporal lobes, specifically involving the amygdala. HSV-1 has a strong predilection for the limbic cortex of the temporal and inferior frontal lobes.

Distractor rationales:
- Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is caused by thiamine (B1) deficiency in chronic alcoholism, damaging mamillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confabulation).
- Anton-Babinski syndrome is visual anosognosia (cortical blindness with denial of blindness) due to bilateral occipital lobe infarction.
- Capgras syndrome is the delusion that familiar people have been replaced by identical impostors.
- Fregoli delusion is the belief that different people are actually a single person in disguise.

question: A 55-year-old executive undergoes surgical resection of a subfrontal meningioma. Postoperatively, his family notes that he lacks motivation, has difficulty planning his workday, cannot switch between tasks, and demonstrates profound apathy and abulia. Testing confirms poor performance on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test. Which cortical region is primarily responsible for these executive cognitive functions?

options.text: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Orbitofrontal cortex
Ventromedial prefrontal cortex
Anterior cingulate cortex
Premotor cortex

explanation:
The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann areas 9 and 46) is primarily responsible for executive cognitive functions: abstract reasoning, problem-solving, cognitive flexibility, goal-directed behavior, working memory, and mental set-shifting (assessed by the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test). Lesions here cause apathy, abulia, and executive dysfunction.

Distractor rationales:
- Orbitofrontal cortex mediates social behavior, risk assessment, and impulse control; lesions cause disinhibition.
- Ventromedial prefrontal cortex is involved in processing emotion, value-based decision making, and moral judgment.
- Anterior cingulate cortex mediates motivation and attention; lesions can produce akinetic mutism.
- Premotor cortex (Brodmann 6) coordinates complex motor programming and postural adjustments.

question: A 34-year-old construction worker survives a severe penetrating injury to the anterior skull base. Physically he recovers completely, but his coworkers note he is 'no longer himself.' Previously polite and conscientious, he is now foul-mouthed, highly impulsive, easily angered, and prone to reckless financial gambling. He shows no remorse when offending others. The damaged brain region corresponds to which of the following?

options.text: Orbitofrontal cortex
Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Primary somatosensory cortex
Broca area
Hippocampus

explanation:
This classic presentation (personality change, disinhibition, social inappropriateness, impulsivity, loss of empathy, resembling the famous case of Phineas Gage) results from damage to the orbitofrontal cortex / ventromedial prefrontal cortex. The orbitofrontal cortex has extensive connections with the limbic system (amygdala) and regulates emotional responses, impulse control, and social etiquette.

Distractor rationales:
- Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex damage causes executive dysfunction, working memory deficits, and apathy rather than impulsive disinhibition.
- Primary somatosensory cortex damage causes contralateral sensory deficits.
- Broca area damage causes expressive aphasia.
- Hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia without disinhibited sociopathy.

question: During a neuroanatomy lab, students examine the dorsal surface of the midbrain tectum. The instructor points to the paired superior colliculi and inferior colliculi. Which of the following accurately describes the primary functional role of the superior colliculi?

options.text: Directing eye movements and head orientation toward visual stimuli
Relaying auditory information from the lateral lemniscus to the medial geniculate body
Secreting melatonin in response to circadian light signals
Buffering emotional memory via connections to the stria terminalis
Mediating pain transmission via descending enkephalinergic projections

explanation:
The superior colliculi form the rostral half of the midbrain tectum (quadrigeminal plate) and mediate visual reflexes, coordination of saccadic eye movements, and reflexive head turning toward sudden visual or auditory stimuli.

Distractor rationales:
- Inferior colliculi relay auditory signals from the lateral lemniscus to the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) of the thalamus.
- The pineal gland secretes melatonin.
- The amygdala and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis buffer emotional responses and anxiety.
- The periaqueductal gray (PAG) mediates descending pain modulation.

question: A 68-year-old man presents with acute double vision and left-sided body weakness. Physical examination reveals an ipsilateral (right-sided) complete third cranial nerve palsy with ptosis and a fixed, dilated pupil, along with contralateral (left-sided) spastic hemiparesis and hyperreflexia. A non-contrast head CT localizes the lesion to the ventral midbrain. This neurovascular syndrome is known as which of the following?

options.text: Weber syndrome
Benedikt syndrome
Claude syndrome
Wallenberg syndrome
Millard-Gubler syndrome

explanation:
Weber syndrome (superior alternating hemiplegia) is a midbrain vascular syndrome typically caused by occlusion of paramedian penetrating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) or basilar bifurcation. The lesion affects the crus cerebri (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, causing contralateral hemiparesis) and the fascicles of the oculomotor nerve (CN III, causing ipsilateral CN III palsy with down-and-out eye and mydriasis).

Distractor rationales:
- Benedikt syndrome involves the midbrain tegmentum (CN III palsy + red nucleus/cerebellothalamic tract causing contralateral tremor/ataxia).
- Claude syndrome involves midbrain tegmentum (CN III palsy + superior cerebellar peduncle ataxia without hemiparesis).
- Wallenberg syndrome is lateral medullary infarction (PICA occlusion).
- Millard-Gubler syndrome is ventral pontine syndrome (CN VI and VII palsies + contralateral hemiplegia).

question: A 50-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive. Emergency CT angiogram shows a ruptured saccular aneurysm arising from the posterior communicating artery (PComA) junction. She develops sudden right ptosis and a fixed, dilated pupil. Which anatomical space did the aneurysm expand into to compress the oculomotor nerve near its exit?

options.text: Interpeduncular fossa
Pre-olivary sulcus
Cerebellopontine angle
Foramen cecum of the medulla
Optic canal

explanation:
The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the midbrain on its ventral aspect within the interpeduncular fossa (the depression between the two cerebral peduncles). The posterior communicating artery courses immediately superior and lateral to CN III near the tentorial notch. A PComA aneurysm characteristically compresses CN III from above, affecting the superficial parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers first (pupillary dilation and sluggish light reflex) followed by somatic motor fibers.

Distractor rationales:
- Pre-olivary sulcus contains CN XII.
- Cerebellopontine angle contains CN VII and VIII.
- Foramen cecum of medulla is the midline depression at the upper end of the anterior median fissure.
- Optic canal transmits CN II and ophthalmic artery.

question: A 48-year-old male presents with unilateral facial palsy, hyperacusis, loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and horizontal gaze palsy when attempting to look toward the side of the lesion. An MRI localizes a small ischemic infarct to the pontomedullary junction. Which group of cranial nerves emerges from the brainstem at or near this junction?

options.text: CN VI, CN VII, and CN VIII
CN III, CN IV, and CN V
CN IX, CN X, and CN XII
CN I and CN II
CN IV and CN V

explanation:
Cranial nerves VI (abducens), VII (facial), and VIII (vestibulocochlear) emerge at the pontomedullary junction. CN VI emerges most medially, immediately above the medullary pyramid; CN VII emerges intermediate in the cerebellopontine sulcus; and CN VIII emerges most laterally in the cerebellopontine angle.

Distractor rationales:
- CN III emerges from midbrain interpeduncular fossa; CN IV emerges dorsal midbrain; CN V emerges mid-pons.
- CN IX and X emerge from post-olivary sulcus; CN XII emerges from pre-olivary sulcus.
- CN I enters the olfactory bulb; CN II enters the diencephalon at the optic chiasm.
- CN IV exits dorsal midbrain; CN V exits anterolateral pons.

question: A 54-year-old woman presents with progressive right-sided sensorineural hearing loss, unsteadiness, and constant high-pitched tinnitus over 2 years. Recently, she noted mild numbness over her right cheek and a diminished corneal reflex on the right. MRI reveals a 3.5 cm contrast-enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle extending into the internal acoustic meatus. This tumor originates from which cell type?

options.text: Schwann cells
Oligodendrocytes
Meningothelial cells
Astrocytes
Microglial cells

explanation:
This patient has a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), a benign tumor of Schwann cells (neural crest origin) arising from the vestibular portion of cranial nerve VIII. Because the tumor grows within the cerebellopontine angle, it first compresses CN VIII (sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, dysequilibrium), then expands to compress CN VII and CN V (causing facial numbness and loss of corneal reflex afferents).

Distractor rationales:
- Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons in the central nervous system; schwannomas arise from PNS myelin (Schwann cells).
- Meningothelial cells give rise to meningiomas (which can also occur in CPA, but histologically show psammoma bodies and whorls, and do not widen the internal acoustic canal).
- Astrocytes give rise to astrocytomas / glioblastomas.
- Microglia are CNS resident macrophages.

question: A 73-year-old man presents with sudden slurred speech. On examination, when asked to protrude his tongue, it deviates sharply to the right side. Fasciculations and mild atrophy of the right half of the tongue are noted. Muscle strength in the limbs is completely normal. An MRI reveals a small paramedian medullary infarct. Damage to which nerve rootlets in which groove accounts for this tongue deviation?

options.text: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) in the pre-olivary sulcus
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) in the post-olivary sulcus
Vagus nerve (CN X) in the retro-olivary sulcus
Accessory nerve (CN XI) in the lateral funiculus
Facial nerve (CN VII) in the pontomedullary groove

explanation:
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges as a series of rootlets from the pre-olivary (anterolateral) sulcus of the medulla, located between the pyramid (ventrally) and the olive (dorsolaterally). CN XII provides somatic motor innervation to the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus, CN X). A lower motor neuron lesion of CN XII causes flaccid paralysis, atrophy, and fasciculations of the ipsilateral genioglossus muscle; upon protrusion, the unopposed contralateral genioglossus pushes the tongue TOWARD the side of the lesion ('lick your lesion').

Distractor rationales:
- CN IX emerges from post-olivary sulcus; provides sensation to posterior 1/3 of tongue, not motor to tongue.
- CN X innervates palatoglossus and pharyngeal muscles; damage causes uvular deviation away from lesion.
- CN XI innervates SCM and trapezius.
- CN VII innervates muscles of facial expression and carries anterior 2/3 taste.

question: A 60-year-old man presents with right arm and leg weakness following an ischemic stroke. The neurologist explains that voluntary motor control travels via the corticospinal tract, which decussates at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord. What percentage of corticospinal fibers decussate at the pyramidal decussation, and which tract do they form?

options.text: Approximately 85-90% decussate to form the lateral corticospinal tract
Approximately 50% decussate to form the anterior corticospinal tract
Approximately 10-15% decussate to form the rubrospinal tract
100% decussate to form the tectospinal tract
0% decussate; all fibers descend ipsilaterally

explanation:
At the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla, approximately 85-90% of descending corticospinal fibers cross the ventral midline to enter the contralateral lateral funiculus of the spinal cord, forming the lateral corticospinal tract. This tract is responsible for fractionation of movement and voluntary control of distal limb musculature. The remaining 10-15% of fibers descend uncrossed in the anterior funiculus as the anterior (ventral) corticospinal tract, which controls axial and proximal limb girdle muscles and decussates near its target spinal cord segment.

Distractor rationales:
- 50% is incorrect; the vast majority cross.
- Rubrospinal tract arises from the red nucleus of the midbrain.
- Tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus.
- The corticospinal tract does cross; unilateral hemispheric lesions cause contralateral weakness.

question: An anatomist is demonstrating the cranial meninges on a cadaveric specimen. She points out that the cranial dura mater consists of two distinct layers: an outer periosteal layer and an inner meningeal layer. At specific locations, the meningeal layer reflects inward to form partitions between brain compartments. Which dural reflection separates the occipital lobes of the cerebrum from the cerebellum?

options.text: Tentorium cerebelli
Falx cerebri
Falx cerebelli
Diaphragma sellae
Tentorial notch

explanation:
The tentorium cerebelli is a crescent-shaped horizontal dural reflection that arches over the posterior cranial fossa, separating the occipital lobes of the cerebral hemispheres from the underlying cerebellum. It divides the cranial cavity into supratentorial and infratentorial compartments.

Distractor rationales:
- Falx cerebri is a sickle-shaped vertical fold lying in the longitudinal fissure between the two cerebral hemispheres.
- Falx cerebelli is a small vertical fold in the posterior cranial fossa partially separating the cerebellar hemispheres.
- Diaphragma sellae forms the roof over the sella turcica, covering the pituitary gland.
- Tentorial notch (incisura) is the U-shaped opening in the anterior edge of the tentorium through which the midbrain passes.

question: A 28-year-old man involved in a high-speed motorcycle crash develops rapidly worsening intracranial pressure from a traumatic right temporal epidural hematoma. The medial aspect of his right temporal lobe herniates downward through the tentorial notch. Which combination of anatomical structures is most directly compressed by this herniation?

options.text: Ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) and posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
Ipsilateral abducens nerve (CN VI) and anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
Contralateral trochlear nerve (CN IV) and middle cerebral artery (MCA)
Ipsilateral optic chiasm and basilar artery
Bilateral olfactory bulbs and anterior communicating artery

explanation:
Uncal (transtentorial) herniation occurs when expanding supratentorial mass lesions force the uncus of the medial temporal lobe medially and downward through the tentorial incisura (notch). This directly compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III, resulting in ipsilateral pupil dilation and ptosis) and the ipsilateral posterior cerebral artery (PCA, leading to occipital lobe infarction and contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing). Further downward displacement causes Kernohan notch phenomenon (false localizing hemiparesis) and fatal Duret hemorrhages in the brainstem.

Distractor rationales:
- CN VI and ACA are not adjacent to the tentorial notch (ACA is affected in subfalcine herniation).
- CN IV is dorsal and MCA is lateral in the Sylvian fissure.
- Optic chiasm is suprasellar, well anterior to the tentorial notch.
- Olfactory bulbs lie on the cribriform plate of the anterior fossa.

question: During a diagnostic lumbar puncture or cisternography, radiologic contrast is followed through the subarachnoid spaces and cisterns. Which of the following subarachnoid cisterns is the largest in volume, located between the inferior surface of the cerebellum and the dorsal surface of the medulla oblongata, and directly receives CSF from the foramen of Magendie?

options.text: Cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern)
Interpeduncular cistern
Ambient (quadrigeminal) cistern
Prepontine cistern
Chiasmatic cistern

explanation:
The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern in the cranial cavity. It is situated in the posterior cranial fossa between the inferior cerebellar vermis/hemispheres and the dorsal surface of the medulla oblongata. It directly receives CSF from the fourth ventricle via the median aperture (foramen of Magendie).

Distractor rationales:
- Interpeduncular cistern is located between the two cerebral peduncles on the ventral midbrain.
- Ambient cistern wraps around the midbrain tegmentum and tectum (quadrigeminal cistern).
- Prepontine cistern lies ventral to the basilar pons.
- Chiasmatic cistern lies adjacent to the optic chiasm.

question: An anesthesiologist is administering epidural anesthesia to a laboring mother at the L3-L4 interspace. A medical student asks how the spinal epidural space compares anatomically to the cranial epidural space. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The spinal epidural space is a true space containing adipose tissue and a venous plexus, whereas the cranial epidural space is a potential space
Both the spinal and cranial epidural spaces are true spaces containing cerebrospinal fluid
The spinal epidural space is a potential space between periosteum and arachnoid, whereas the cranial space is a true space containing arterial sinuses
The spinal epidural space is continuous with the subarachnoid space via arachnoid granulations
The cranial epidural space contains fatty tissue and lymphatics, whereas the spinal epidural space is devoid of fat

explanation:
In the spinal canal, the dura mater is separated from the vertebral periosteum by a real anatomical space: the spinal epidural space, filled with loose adipose connective tissue and the extensive internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus). In contrast, in the cranium, the outer periosteal layer of the dura mater is intimately fused to the inner table of the skull bones; therefore, the cranial epidural space is normally only a potential space that opens pathologically when blood strips the dura away from bone (as in an epidural hematoma).

Distractor rationales:
- Epidural spaces do not contain CSF (CSF is confined to the subarachnoid space).
- Cranial epidural space is not a true space; it is potential.
- The epidural space is completely separate from the subarachnoid space by the arachnoid and dura.
- Cranial epidural space does not contain fat; spinal epidural space does.

question: A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma presents with back pain and lower extremity weakness. MRI demonstrates multiple osteoblastic vertebral lesions and epidural spinal cord compression, as well as a solitary brain metastasis. Biopsy confirms metastatic adenocarcinoma. The primary route of retrograde tumor embolization from the pelvis to the spine and cranial cavity bypasses the inferior vena cava via which anatomical structure?

options.text: Batson internal vertebral venous plexus
Azygos and hemiazygos venous system
Portal venous system
Superior sagittal sinus directly
Thoracic duct lymphatic channels

explanation:
Batson venous plexus (internal vertebral venous plexus) is an extensive, valveless network of veins located within the spinal epidural space. It communicates freely with the pelvic venous plexus (prostatic venous plexus via pelvic veins) and the intracranial dural venous sinuses. Because it lacks valves, increases in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., coughing, straining) cause retrograde blood flow, allowing pelvic tumors (especially prostate carcinoma) and infections to seed the vertebral bodies and cranium directly without passing through the inferior vena cava or lungs.

Distractor rationales:
- Azygos system drains posterior thorax and connects to SVC, but Batson plexus is the primary valveless epidural route.
- Portal system drains abdominal viscera to the liver.
- Superior sagittal sinus is intracranial; it receives blood from Batson plexus superiorly, but is not the primary bridging plexus in the pelvis.
- Thoracic duct carries lymph from lower body to left subclavian vein.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with neck pain and tingling radiating into his right shoulder and lateral arm. An MRI of the cervical spine demonstrates a posterolateral disc herniation between the C4 and C5 cervical vertebrae. Which spinal nerve root exits through the intervertebral foramen between C4 and C5 and is most likely compressed by this disc herniation?

options.text: C5 spinal nerve root
C4 spinal nerve root
C6 spinal nerve root
C3 spinal nerve root
C8 spinal nerve root

explanation:
In the cervical spine, there are 8 cervical spinal nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae. Nerve roots C1 through C7 exit the intervertebral foramina ABOVE their correspondingly numbered vertebrae (e.g., C1 exits above C1 vertebra, C2 above C2, ..., and C5 exits ABOVE the C5 vertebra, which is between C4 and C5). Nerve root C8 exits between C7 and T1. From T1 downward, all spinal nerve roots exit BELOW their correspondingly numbered vertebrae.

Distractor rationales:
- C4 exits between C3 and C4.
- C6 exits between C5 and C6.
- C3 exits between C2 and C3.
- C8 exits between C7 and T1.

question: A histology resident is examining cross-sections of the cerebral cortex versus the spinal cord. She compares the structural distribution of gray matter and white matter. Which of the following accurately describes this arrangement?

options.text: In the cerebral cortex, gray matter is located superficially on the surface with white matter deep; in the spinal cord, white matter is on the periphery and gray matter forms an inner butterfly core
In both the cerebral cortex and spinal cord, gray matter is located entirely centrally surrounded by outer white matter
In both the cerebral cortex and spinal cord, white matter is located superficially and gray matter is deep
In the cerebral cortex, white matter forms the outer layers I-III and gray matter forms layers IV-VI
In the spinal cord, white matter forms the central canal lining and gray matter forms the dorsal columns

explanation:
In the brain (cerebrum and cerebellum), gray matter (containing neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses) forms the superficial outer cortex (layers I-VI in neocortex), while white matter (myelinated axon tracts) lies deep, surrounding subcortical gray nuclei (basal ganglia, thalamus). In the spinal cord, this organization is inverted: white matter tracts (dorsal, lateral, and anterior funiculi) form the outer periphery, while gray matter forms an inner, H-shaped or butterfly-shaped central core containing dorsal, intermediate, and ventral horns.

Distractor rationales:
- Cerebral cortex has gray matter on the outside, not centrally.
- Cortical layers I-VI are all components of gray matter.
- Spinal cord white matter is peripheral; central canal is lined by ependyma surrounded by central gray matter.

question: During a pathological examination of a coronally sectioned brain, a pathologist identifies the corpus striatum. Which anatomical components combine to form the striatum, and which components form the lentiform nucleus?

options.text: Striatum = Caudate + Putamen; Lentiform nucleus = Putamen + Globus pallidus
Striatum = Putamen + Globus pallidus; Lentiform nucleus = Caudate + Subthalamic nucleus
Striatum = Caudate + Substantia nigra; Lentiform nucleus = Putamen + Claustrum
Striatum = Globus pallidus + Thalamus; Lentiform nucleus = Caudate + Amygdala
Striatum = Caudate + Putamen + Globus pallidus; Lentiform nucleus = Subthalamic nucleus + Substantia nigra

explanation:
In basal ganglia terminology:
- The STRIATUM (neostriatum) consists of the CAUDATE NUCLEUS and the PUTAMEN, which develop from the telencephalon and are structurally bridged by cellular bridges traversing the internal capsule.
- The LENTIFORM (lenticular) NUCLEUS is a lens-shaped anatomic grouping comprising the PUTAMEN and the GLOBUS PALLIDUS (external and internal segments).
Thus, the putamen belongs to both the striatum and the lentiform nucleus.

Distractor rationales:
- Putamen + Globus pallidus is the lentiform nucleus, not the striatum.
- Substantia nigra is in the midbrain and is not part of the striatum anatomically.
- Globus pallidus + Thalamus is not a recognized anatomical unit.
- The three together (caudate + putamen + globus pallidus) are called the corpus striatum.

question: A 66-year-old retired schoolteacher presents with sudden reading difficulty following an embolic stroke. On examination, when given a printed paragraph, he cannot read a single word (alexia). However, when handed a pen and paper, he writes a coherent, grammatically flawless letter to his daughter, but moments later cannot read what he just wrote (alexia without agraphia). An MRI reveals an infarction in the left occipital cortex and which specific part of the corpus callosum?

options.text: Splenium of the corpus callosum
Genu of the corpus callosum
Rostrum of the corpus callosum
Body of the corpus callosum
Anterior commissure

explanation:
Alexia without agraphia (pure alexia) is a classic disconnection syndrome caused by infarction in the territory of the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA). The stroke damages the left visual cortex (producing a right homonymous hemianopia) AND the SPLENIUM of the corpus callosum. Visual information from the intact right visual cortex reaches the right occipital cortex, but because the splenium is damaged, it cannot cross to the dominant left hemisphere language area (angular gyrus) for word recognition (causing alexia). Because the left angular gyrus itself is intact, the patient can write normally (no agraphia).

Distractor rationales:
- Genu connects anterior frontal lobes and mediates executive/motor integration.
- Rostrum connects ventral frontal lobes.
- Body of corpus callosum connects motor, sensory, and parietal cortices.
- Anterior commissure connects temporal lobes and olfactory structures.

question: A 24-year-old medical student is reviewing cortical landmarks. She identifies the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) and retracts the temporal operculum to view the superior temporal plane. Two oblique transverse convolutions are visible running anterolaterally from the circular sulcus. These gyri (Heschl gyri) correspond to which functional area?

options.text: Primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42)
Primary gustatory cortex (Brodmann area 43)
Primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17)
Primary olfactory cortex (Brodmann area 28)
Primary vestibular cortex (Brodmann area 2)

explanation:
Transverse temporal gyri of Heschl (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) represent the primary auditory cortex. They are located on the superior surface of the superior temporal gyrus, buried inside the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure). They receive tonotopically organized auditory projections from the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) of the thalamus via the sublenticular part of the internal capsule.

Distractor rationales:
- Primary gustatory cortex (Brodmann 43) is located in the insular cortex and adjacent operculum.
- Primary visual cortex (Brodmann 17) is in the banks of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe.
- Primary olfactory cortex is in the piriform cortex and uncus in the anterior medial temporal lobe.
- Primary vestibular sensations project to parietal and temporoparietal areas.

question: During the third week of embryonic human development, the notochord secretes molecular signals that induce the overlying ectoderm to differentiate into the neuroectoderm, forming the neural plate. Which of the following molecular mechanisms mediates this embryonic neural induction?

options.text: Inhibition of Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4 (BMP-4) by noggin and chordin
Activation of Wnt signaling in the hypoblast
Direct stimulation of TGF-beta receptors by retinoic acid
Downregulation of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) by fibroblast growth factor
Overexpression of Notch-1 by endodermal derivatives

explanation:
Primary neural induction occurs when the notochord and prechordal mesoderm secrete BMP antagonists (specifically noggin, chordin, and follistatin). In the absence of BMP antagonists, BMP-4 signaling causes ectoderm to differentiate into surface epidermis. Secretion of noggin and chordin binds and inhibits BMP-4, allowing the default neuroectodermal differentiation program to proceed and forming the neural plate.

Distractor rationales:
- Wnt signaling patterns anterior-posterior polarity, but does not initiate initial neural plate induction.
- Retinoic acid is involved in hindbrain and spinal cord craniocaudal patterning.
- Sonic Hedgehog is secreted by the notochord to induce ventral floor plate and motor neurons, not initial neural plate induction.
- Notch signaling regulates neuronal vs glial fate decisions during proliferation.

question: During normal embryonic development, the neural groove deepens and the neural folds fuse in the midline to form the neural tube. Closure begins in the cervical region and progresses bidirectionally. On which embryonic days do the anterior (cranial) and posterior (caudal) neuropores normally complete closure?

options.text: Anterior neuropore closes on day 25; posterior neuropore closes on day 27
Anterior neuropore closes on day 14; posterior neuropore closes on day 21
Anterior neuropore closes on day 28; posterior neuropore closes on day 35
Anterior neuropore closes on day 40; posterior neuropore closes on day 42
Both neuropores close simultaneously on day 21

explanation:
Neurulation in humans proceeds with the anterior (cranial or rostral) neuropore closing on approximately embryonic day 25 (allowing the brain vesicles to expand), followed shortly by the posterior (caudal) neuropore closing on embryonic day 27 (completing the spinal cord tube). Failure of anterior neuropore closure leads to anencephaly; failure of posterior neuropore closure leads to spina bifida and myelomeningocele.

Distractor rationales:
- Day 14 is the time of gastrulation and primitive streak formation.
- Day 28-35 is during vesicle differentiation and limb bud outgrowth.
- Day 40-42 is after primary neurulation has finished.
- The neuropores do not close simultaneously; the anterior closes approximately 2 days before the posterior.

question: A newborn is diagnosed with Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) and Waardenburg syndrome (heterochromia iridis, white forelock, sensorineural deafness). The physician explains that both disorders stem from abnormal migration and development of neural crest cells. Which of the following adult tissues is also derived from neural crest cells?

options.text: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells
Anterior pituitary corticotrophs
Nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs
Motor neurons of the ventral spinal cord
Oligodendrocytes of the optic nerve

explanation:
Neural crest cells (the 'fourth germ layer') originate from the lateral margins of the neural plate and migrate extensively throughout the embryo. Neural crest derivatives include: adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells), melanocytes, Schwann cells, dorsal root ganglia (DRG), autonomic ganglia, pia and arachnoid mater, branchial arch skeletal/connective tissues, thyroid C (parafollicular) cells, and aorticopulmonary septum. Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest migration into the myenteric/submucosal plexus of the colon.

Distractor rationales:
- Anterior pituitary is derived from oral surface ectoderm (Rathke pouch).
- Nucleus pulposus is the embryonic remnant of the notochord.
- Motor neurons of the ventral spinal cord derive from the basal plate of the neural tube.
- Oligodendrocytes derive from neuroepithelial cells of the neural tube.

question: By the fifth week of human embryonic development, the three primary brain vesicles subdivide into five secondary brain vesicles. Which secondary vesicle gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres and the lateral ventricles, and which primary vesicle did it originate from?

options.text: Telencephalon, originating from the Prosencephalon
Diencephalon, originating from the Prosencephalon
Mesencephalon, originating from the Rhombencephalon
Metencephalon, originating from the Mesencephalon
Myelencephalon, originating from the Rhombencephalon

explanation:
At 5 weeks, the primary vesicles subdivide:
- Prosencephalon (forebrain) divides into the TELENCEPHALON (gives rise to cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, and lateral ventricles) and DIENCEPHALON (gives rise to epithalamus, thalamus, hypothalamus, retina/optic nerve, and 3rd ventricle).
- Mesencephalon remains undivided (gives rise to midbrain and cerebral aqueduct).
- Rhombencephalon (hindbrain) divides into Metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and Myelencephalon (medulla oblongata).

Distractor rationales:
- Diencephalon gives rise to thalamus/hypothalamus and 3rd ventricle.
- Mesencephalon originates from the mesencephalon primary vesicle, not rhombencephalon.
- Metencephalon originates from the rhombencephalon, not mesencephalon.
- Myelencephalon gives rise to the medulla oblongata, not cerebral cortex.

question: An MRI of an infant demonstrates congenital hypoplasia of the thalamus and optic chiasm. In terms of embryonic lineage, both the dorsal thalamus and the neuroretina develop from which secondary brain vesicle?

options.text: Diencephalon
Telencephalon
Mesencephalon
Metencephalon
Myelencephalon

explanation:
The diencephalon gives rise to the epithalamus (pineal gland), thalamus, hypothalamus, mamillary bodies, and neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary), as well as outpocketings called the optic vesicles, which form the optic cup, retina, and optic nerve (CN II). This is why the optic nerve is considered an extension of the central nervous system (myelinated by oligodendrocytes, surrounded by meninges).

Distractor rationales:
- Telencephalon gives rise to cerebral cortex, caudate, putamen, amygdala, and hippocampus.
- Mesencephalon gives rise to midbrain (tectum, tegmentum, crus cerebri).
- Metencephalon gives rise to pons and cerebellum.
- Myelencephalon gives rise to medulla.

question: During brainstem organogenesis, the metencephalon and myelencephalon develop from the rhombencephalon. Which adult brain structures develop directly from the metencephalon?

options.text: Pons and cerebellum
Medulla oblongata and inferior olivary nucleus
Substantia nigra and red nucleus
Hypothalamus and mamillary bodies
Globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus

explanation:
The rhombencephalon (hindbrain) divides into the rostral metencephalon and caudal myelencephalon. The metencephalon forms the pons ventrally and the cerebellum dorsally (via rhombic lip proliferation), and encloses the rostral half of the fourth ventricle. The myelencephalon forms the medulla oblongata and encloses the caudal fourth ventricle.

Distractor rationales:
- Medulla oblongata develops from the myelencephalon.
- Substantia nigra and red nucleus develop from the mesencephalon.
- Hypothalamus and mamillary bodies develop from the diencephalon.
- Globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus develop from the diencephalon/telencephalon.

question: In the developing embryonic spinal cord, the longitudinal groove called the sulcus limitans separates the dorsal alar plate from the ventral basal plate. What are the respective functional fates and primary organizing morphogens for these two plates?

options.text: Alar plate is sensory (induced by BMP/TGF-beta); Basal plate is motor (induced by Sonic Hedgehog)
Alar plate is motor (induced by Sonic Hedgehog); Basal plate is sensory (induced by BMP)
Alar plate is autonomic (induced by Wnt); Basal plate is sensory (induced by Notch)
Alar plate gives rise to white matter; Basal plate gives rise to gray matter
Both alar and basal plates give rise exclusively to sensory interneurons

explanation:
The sulcus limitans divides the embryonic neural tube into the dorsal ALAR plate (sensory, afferent, gives rise to dorsal horn sensory neurons; induced by BMPs and Wnts from the roof plate) and the ventral BASAL plate (motor, efferent, gives rise to ventral horn motor neurons; induced by Sonic Hedgehog / SHH secreted by the notochord and floor plate).

Distractor rationales:
- Basal is motor, not alar.
- Autonomic neurons reside in the intermediate horn (lateral horn T1-L2, S2-S4), but alar is primarily sensory and basal is motor.
- Both plates form gray matter, while surrounding neuroepithelial axons form white matter tracts.
- Basal plate gives rise to motor neurons, not sensory interneurons.

question: During development of the brainstem, the fourth ventricle flares open dorsally like an open book. As a result of this anatomical opening, how are the sensory and motor nuclei arranged in the floor of the fourth ventricle (rhomboid fossa)?

options.text: Motor nuclei lie medially, while sensory nuclei lie laterally
Sensory nuclei lie medially, while motor nuclei lie laterally
Motor nuclei lie dorsally, while sensory nuclei lie ventrally
Motor nuclei lie rostrally, while sensory nuclei lie exclusively caudally
Motor and sensory nuclei are randomly intermingled without spatial organization

explanation:
In the embryonic spinal cord, the alar plate (sensory) is dorsal to the basal plate (motor). However, in the brainstem (pons and medulla), the dorsal roof plate expands laterally to form the thin roof of the fourth ventricle. This flaring opens the dorsal tube like a book: the basal plate motor columns are kept MEDIAL (adjacent to the midline sulcus limitans), while the alar plate sensory columns are displaced LATERALLY. Thus, in the brainstem floor, somatic and visceral motor nuclei are medial, and somatic and visceral sensory nuclei are lateral.

Distractor rationales:
- Sensory nuclei are lateral, not medial.
- Dorsal/ventral orientation was the spinal cord layout before the 4th ventricle flared open.
- Rostral/caudal segregation is not the primary organizing principle; mediolateral segregation is.
- The nuclei are highly organized into distinct functional columns (GSE, SVE, GVE medially; GVA, SVA, GSA, SSA laterally).

question: During neocortical histogenesis, neural progenitor cells proliferate in the ventricular zone and then neuroblasts migrate radially toward the pial surface. Which of the following best describes the migration guide and the layer-by-layer formation sequence of the 6-layered neocortex?

options.text: Migration guided by radial glial cells; cortical layers form in an 'inside-out' sequence (layer VI first, layer II last)
Migration guided by microglia; cortical layers form in an 'outside-in' sequence (layer I first, layer VI last)
Migration guided by oligodendrocytes; layers form simultaneously via clonal expansion
Migration guided by ependymal cilia; layers form from superficial to deep
Migration guided by Schwann cells; layers form randomly without chronological order

explanation:
Neocortical development follows an 'inside-out' pattern: the earliest migrating neuroblasts populate the deepest layers (preplate, subplate, then layer VI and layer V), whereas subsequent waves of neuroblasts migrate past the older cells along elongated radial glial fibers to form the progressively more superficial layers (layer IV, layer III, and finally layer II). Radial glia act both as neural stem cells and as structural scaffold guides.

Distractor rationales:
- Microglia are mesodermal immune scavengers, not guides for radial migration.
- Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons later in development, not during neuroblast migration.
- Ependymal cells line ventricular cavities and do not extend fibers to the pia.
- Schwann cells are in the peripheral nervous system.

question: A 6-month-old male infant is evaluated for intractable infantile spasms, severe developmental delay, and microcephaly. High-resolution brain MRI reveals a completely smooth cerebral surface lacking normal sulci and gyri (agyria), along with an abnormally thick four-layered cortex. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the LIS1 gene. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Lissencephaly (type 1)
Polymicrogyria
Holoprosencephaly
Schizencephaly
Periventricular nodular heterotopia

explanation:
Lissencephaly (type 1, classic 'smooth brain') is a severe malformation of cortical development characterized by the absence of normal gyri and sulci (agyria or pachygyria) and an abnormally thickened cortex with only four disorganized cellular layers instead of six. It is caused by defective arrest of neuronal radial migration, most commonly due to mutations in LIS1 (PAFAH1B1 gene on chromosome 17p13.3, Miller-Dieker syndrome) or DCX (doublecortin on Xq22.3). Affected infants have profound developmental delay, intractable epilepsy, and feeding difficulties.

Distractor rationales:
- Polymicrogyria features an excessive number of tiny, disorganized, fused gyri.
- Holoprosencephaly is failure of the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres.
- Schizencephaly consists of full-thickness clefts extending through the hemisphere lined by gray matter.
- Periventricular nodular heterotopia consists of discrete gray matter clumps lining the ventricular walls.

question: A 19-year-old woman with normal intelligence presents with new-onset focal seizures with impaired awareness. Brain MRI demonstrates multiple, rounded, non-calcified nodules of gray matter isointense to cortex protruding into the lumen of the lateral ventricles bilaterally. Genetic analysis reveals an X-linked dominant loss-of-function mutation in the FLNA gene encoding filamin A. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Periventricular nodular heterotopia
Tuberous sclerosis complex
Sturge-Weber syndrome
Ependymoma
Neurofibromatosis type 1

explanation:
Periventricular nodular heterotopia (PNH) is a disorder of neuronal migration in which a subset of neuroblasts fails to initiate radial migration away from the ventricular neuroepithelium, persisting as subependymal clumps or nodules of normal-appearing neurons lining the walls of the lateral ventricles. It is most commonly caused by X-linked dominant mutations in the FLNA (filamin A) gene, which is essential for actin cytoskeleton remodeling. Hemizygous males typically suffer prenatal lethality; heterozygous females present in adolescence or adulthood with epilepsy and normal or near-normal intelligence.

Distractor rationales:
- Tuberous sclerosis features subependymal nodules that calcify ('candle drippings') and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs), along with cortical tubers and facial angiofibromas (TSC1/TSC2 mutations).
- Sturge-Weber features leptomeningeal angiomas and port-wine stain (GNAQ mutation).
- Ependymoma is an intraventricular neoplasm, typically in the 4th ventricle of children.
- NF1 features café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules.

question: A 1-year-old child born with congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection presents with spastic quadriparesis, microcephaly, and developmental arrest. Brain MRI shows periventricular calcifications and extensive bilateral cobblestone-like cortical irregularity with excessive numbers of small, fused, shallow gyri separated by shallow sulci. This cortical malformation is known as which of the following?

options.text: Polymicrogyria
Lissencephaly
Holoprosencephaly
Anencephaly
Schizencephaly

explanation:
Polymicrogyria is a malformation of cortical development characterized by an excessive number of abnormally small, shallow, fused gyri with a bumpy, pebbled, or cobblestone surface. Histologically, there is disruption of late neuronal migration and laminar organization, often resulting in a disorganized 4-layered or unlayered cortex. Congenital viral infections (especially CMV), intrauterine ischemia, or mutations in GPR56 are prominent causes.

Distractor rationales:
- Lissencephaly features complete absence of gyri (smooth cortex).
- Holoprosencephaly is failure of the forebrain to separate into hemispheres.
- Anencephaly is failure of anterior neuropore closure with absence of calvarium and forebrain.
- Schizencephaly features full-thickness clefts from ventricle to pial surface.

question: An ultrasound of a 20-week fetus reveals a single, monoventricular brain cavity, fusion of the thalami, absence of the midline falx cerebri, hypotelorism, a cleft lip, and a flat nasal bridge. The mother has poorly controlled pregestational diabetes mellitus. Genetic evaluation reveals a mutation in the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway. Which of the following conditions is present?

options.text: Holoprosencephaly
Chiari II malformation
Dandy-Walker malformation
Agenesis of the corpus callosum alone
Encephalocele

explanation:
Holoprosencephaly (HPE) is a complex developmental anomaly resulting from failure of the embryonic prosencephalon (forebrain) to cleave sagitally into bilateral cerebral hemispheres, usually occurring between weeks 5 and 6 of gestation. It is associated with mutations in the SHH gene, Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), Trisomy 18, and maternal diabetes mellitus. Phenotypes range from alobar (most severe: single ventricle, fused thalami, cyclopia, proboscis) to semilobar to lobar (milder facial anomalies such as single central incisor or cleft lip/palate).

Distractor rationales:
- Chiari II features hindbrain herniation and myelomeningocele.
- Dandy-Walker features vermian hypoplasia and enlarged 4th ventricle/posterior fossa.
- Agenesis of the corpus callosum features absent corpus callosum with preserved hemispheric separation (Probst bundles, 'bat-wing' lateral ventricles).
- Encephalocele is a herniation of intracranial contents through a skull defect.

question: A 24-year-old woman presents with occipital headaches that worsen significantly when she sneezes, coughs, or strains during bowel movements. She also notes progressive dizziness and clumsy hand coordination. A sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the brain and cervical spine reveals herniation of the cerebellar tonsils 8 mm below the level of the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal. The cerebellar vermis and 4th ventricle are in normal position. What is the diagnosis, and what associated spinal cord condition should be evaluated?

options.text: Chiari I malformation; evaluate for cervical syringomyelia
Chiari II malformation; evaluate for lumbosacral myelomeningocele
Dandy-Walker malformation; evaluate for fourth ventricle enlargement
Normal pressure hydrocephalus; evaluate for lumbar stenosis
Basilar invagination; evaluate for odontoid hypoplasia

explanation:
Chiari I malformation is defined as downward displacement (ectopia) of the peg-like cerebellar tonsils >5 mm below the foramen magnum into the upper spinal canal. Unlike Chiari II, the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle remain in their normal intracranial position, and it is NOT associated with myelomeningocele. It classically presents in young adults with suboccipital/neck pain aggravated by Valsalva maneuvers (coughing, straining). Between 30% and 50% of patients with Chiari I have an associated cervical SYRINGOMYELIA (fluid collection in the central canal) due to altered pulsatile CSF dynamics at the craniovertebral junction.

Distractor rationales:
- Chiari II involves both cerebellar vermis and tonsils herniation, brainstem descent, and is universally associated with lumbosacral myelomeningocele.
- Dandy-Walker features vermian agenesis and a large posterior fossa cyst.
- NPH presents with the triad of gait disturbance, incontinence, and dementia.
- Basilar invagination involves upward displacement of the cervical spine into the foramen magnum.

question: A newborn delivered at 38 weeks gestation has a large, open, fluid-filled sac on his lower back containing neural placode tissue. He has bilateral clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) and flaccid paraplegia. Head ultrasound reveals downward herniation of the cerebellar vermis and tonsils into the cervical canal, beaking of the tectal plate, and progressive dilation of the lateral ventricles due to aqueductal compression. What malformation complex is present?

options.text: Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari) malformation
Chiari I malformation
Dandy-Walker malformation
Spina bifida occulta
Isolated anencephaly

explanation:
Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari) malformation is characterized by caudal displacement of the cerebellar vermis, cerebellar tonsils, and medulla oblongata through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal. It is virtually ALWAYS associated with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele. The downward traction and crowding in the posterior fossa obstruct CSF outflow at the cerebral aqueduct or fourth ventricle, leading to progressive obstructive hydrocephalus requiring ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting.

Distractor rationales:
- Chiari I involves isolated tonsillar herniation >5 mm, occurs without myelomeningocele, and presents in adolescents/adults.
- Dandy-Walker malformation features an enlarged posterior fossa with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and a cystic 4th ventricle.
- Spina bifida occulta is an asymptomatic bony defect covered by skin without neural herniation.
- Anencephaly is failure of anterior neuropore closure with absence of forebrain and calvarium.

question: A 32-year-old mechanic presents with repeated painless burns on his forearms and fingers while working with hot car engines. Physical examination reveals complete loss of pain and temperature sensation across both shoulders, arms, and upper chest, but light touch, vibration, and joint position senses are completely preserved in the same regions. MRI reveals a fluid-filled cavitation within the cervical spinal cord at C5-T1. Which neural pathway is disrupted to cause this dissociated sensory loss?

options.text: Decussating second-order fibers in the anterior white commissure
Ascending first-order fibers in the fasciculus cuneatus
Ascending first-order fibers in the fasciculus gracilis
Descending upper motor neurons in the lateral corticospinal tract
Primary afferent fibers in the dorsal root ganglion

explanation:
This is the classic presentation of syringomyelia (fluid-filled syrinx in the central canal of the spinal cord, most commonly cervical C8-T1). As the cavity expands, it first compresses and destroys the decussating spinothalamic (ALS) second-order axons as they cross the midline in the ANTERIOR WHITE COMMISSURE. This produces a bilateral, 'cape-like' (dermatomal) loss of pain and temperature sensation across the shoulders and arms. Because the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) run in the posterior funiculus away from the central canal, vibration and proprioception are spared, producing dissociated sensory loss.

Distractor rationales:
- Fasciculus cuneatus carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from upper limbs; these are intact.
- Fasciculus gracilis carries fine touch and proprioception from lower limbs.
- Lateral corticospinal tract carries descending motor commands; involvement causes spastic paresis (occurs only late if syrinx expands massively).
- DRG carries primary afferents; compression would cause non-dissociated loss of all modalities in a dermatome.

question: Over the next two years, the syringomyelia in the previously described patient expands radially within the cervical cord. He now develops progressive bilateral weakness, muscle wasting, and fasciculations involving the intrinsic muscles of both hands. He also develops a mild right-sided ptosis and miosis (Horner syndrome). Which structures have now been invaded by the expanding syrinx?

options.text: Anterior horn motor neurons and lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) sympathetics
Posterior funiculus and dorsal root entry zone
Lateral funiculus alone
Corticobulbar tracts in the genu
Nucleus gracilis in the medulla

explanation:
As a cervical syrinx expands ventrolaterally, it invades the ANTERIOR HORNS of the spinal cord gray matter (Rexed lamina IX), damaging lower motor neurons and causing flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and hyporeflexia in the hands and arms (LMN deficit). Furthermore, extension into the INTERMEDIOLATERAL CELL COLUMN (lateral horn T1-L2) damages preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies, disrupting the sympathetic chain to the head and causing ipsilateral or bilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

Distractor rationales:
- Posterior funiculus damage causes loss of vibration/proprioception, not muscle wasting.
- Lateral funiculus alone contains corticospinal tracts (UMN signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia), not LMN wasting/fasciculations.
- Corticobulbar tracts are in the brainstem, not cervical cord.
- Nucleus gracilis is in the caudal medulla, not cervical cord.

question: A routine physical examination of a healthy 16-year-old boy reveals a small, 2 cm patch of coarse hair and a subtle skin dimple over the lumbar midline at L5-S1. He has completely normal lower extremity strength, intact sensation, normal deep tendon reflexes, and normal bowel/bladder control. A lumbar spine X-ray reveals failure of fusion of the posterior vertebral arches of L5 and S1, but the dura and arachnoid are completely intact within the bony canal. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Spina bifida occulta
Meningocele
Myelomeningocele
Myeloschisis
Caudal regression syndrome

explanation:
Spina bifida occulta is the mildest form of neural tube defect, characterized by failure of the caudal neural arches (vertebral arches) of one or more vertebrae to fuse in the midline, with normal development and closure of the underlying spinal cord, dura, and skin. It occurs in up to 10-20% of the normal population (most commonly at L5-S1) and is typically asymptomatic, identified incidentally by a cutaneous marker (tuft of hair, skin dimple, hemangioma, or lipoma). Maternal serum AFP is normal.

Distractor rationales:
- Meningocele involves herniation of the meninges through the vertebral defect as a visible fluid-filled cyst.
- Myelomeningocele involves herniation of both meninges and neural tissue (spinal cord/roots) with neurological deficits.
- Myeloschisis is the most severe form where the neural plate remains wide open to the external environment.
- Caudal regression syndrome is severe sacral agenesis associated with maternal diabetes.

question: A newborn delivered by uncomplicated vaginal delivery has a round, skin-covered, cystic mass in the lumbar region. Transillumination of the mass shows clear fluid with no solid neural elements inside. Neurological examination of the infant shows normal lower extremity movements, intact anal sphincter tone, and normal withdrawal reflexes. MRI confirms herniation of the dura mater and arachnoid mater through a bony defect in the posterior spine, with the spinal cord lying entirely within the spinal canal. What is this condition?

options.text: Meningocele
Spina bifida occulta
Myelomeningocele
Sacrococcygeal teratoma
Lipomyelomeningocele

explanation:
A meningocele is a neural tube defect in which the meninges (dura mater and arachnoid mater) herniate through a posterior vertebral bony defect, forming a CSF-filled cystic sac covered by skin or a thin membrane. Crucially, the spinal cord and nerve roots remain completely inside the vertebral canal and are NOT present within the herniated sac. Consequently, neurological examination of the lower extremities is typically normal.

Distractor rationales:
- Spina bifida occulta does not have a herniated external cystic sac.
- Myelomeningocele contains spinal cord and nerve roots within the herniated sac and causes motor/sensory deficits.
- Sacrococcygeal teratoma is a germ cell tumor arising from remnants of the primitive streak at the coccyx (contains mixed tissue layers: hair, bone, teeth).
- Lipomyelomeningocele contains lipomatous tissue tethering the cord.

question: A 2-day-old infant with a severe lumbar myelomeningocele undergoes surgical repair. The parents are counseled regarding potential long-term complications. Which of the following constellations of clinical abnormalities is most commonly associated with a lumbar myelomeningocele?

options.text: Neurogenic bladder/bowel, lower extremity paraparesis, clubfoot (talipes equinovarus), and Chiari II malformation
Hyperreflexia in all four extremities, intact bladder sensation, and Chiari I malformation
Polycythemia, hypertension, and isolated sensory loss in upper extremities
Facial nerve palsy, cleft palate, and normal spinal cord function
Precocious puberty, bilateral cataracts, and normal bladder function

explanation:
Myelomeningocele (the most severe viable neural tube defect) involves herniation of both the meninges and the spinal cord/cauda equina roots through a vertebral defect. Because neural tissue is disrupted, patients suffer lower extremity flaccid paralysis/paresis, sensory loss matching the lesion level, neurogenic bladder (urinary retention/incontinence), fecal incontinence, and musculoskeletal deformities like talipes equinovarus (clubfoot). In >90% of cases, it is associated with Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus.

Distractor rationales:
- Upper extremity hyperreflexia is an upper cervical/brainstem finding; myelomeningocele produces LMN deficits in legs.
- Polycythemia and hypertension are not related.
- Cranial nerve VII palsy and cleft palate are not typical features.
- Precocious puberty and cataracts are unrelated to myelomeningocele.

question: A 28-year-old primigravida undergoes routine second-trimester screening at 16 weeks gestation. Her maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) is markedly elevated at 4.2 multiples of the median (MoM). Fetal ultrasonography confirms a singleton gestation and reveals a flattened frontal skull contour ('lemon sign') and a curved, anteriorly displaced cerebellum ('banana sign'). What subsequent diagnostic finding in the amniotic fluid confirms an open neural tube defect?

options.text: Elevated amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein and detectable acetylcholinesterase (AChE)
Low amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein and elevated bilirubin
Elevated human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and low estriol
Presence of meconium and elevated alkaline phosphatase
Elevated fetal hemoglobin and low creatinine

explanation:
Open neural tube defects (such as myelomeningocele and anencephaly) allow fetal cerebrospinal and vascular fluids to leak directly into the amniotic cavity, resulting in markedly elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) and amniotic fluid AFP (AFAFP). The presence of ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE (AChE) in the amniotic fluid is a highly specific confirmatory test, because AChE is a neuronal enzyme that leaks into amniotic fluid only when neural tissue is directly exposed. Ultrasonography reveals the 'lemon sign' (inward scalloping of frontal bones) and 'banana sign' (cerebellum compressed into posterior fossa) characteristic of Chiari II.

Distractor rationales:
- Low AFP is seen in Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) and Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome).
- Elevated hCG and low estriol is part of the quad screen for Down syndrome, not specific for NTD.
- Meconium and alkaline phosphatase indicate fetal distress or bowel obstruction.
- Fetal hemoglobin is tested in fetomaternal hemorrhage (Kleihauer-Betke test).

question: A 26-year-old woman with a history of epilepsy managed with carbamazepine presents for preconception counseling. She plans to conceive within the next few months. Which of the following vitamin supplements and dosages is recommended to significantly reduce the risk of neural tube defects in her offspring?

options.text: Folic acid (vitamin B9) 4 mg daily, initiated at least 1 month prior to conception
Folic acid 0.4 mg daily, initiated after confirmation of pregnancy
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) 10 mg daily, initiated at 12 weeks gestation
Vitamin A 50,000 IU daily, initiated prior to conception
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 100 mg daily, initiated during the second trimester

explanation:
Periconceptional folic acid (vitamin B9) supplementation dramatically reduces the incidence of neural tube defects by supporting DNA synthesis, methylation, and cell division during rapid neural tube closure (which occurs by day 28, often before a woman realizes she is pregnant). For women at average risk, the standard dose is 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily. However, for women at HIGH RISK (e.g., prior child with NTD, or taking antifolate anti-seizure medications like carbamazepine or valproate), the recommended dose is 4 mg daily, started at least 1 month prior to conception and continued through the first trimester.

Distractor rationales:
- 0.4 mg daily is for low-risk women; this patient takes carbamazepine (high risk) and starting after confirmation is often too late (tube closes by day 28).
- Vitamin B12 does not replace folate and 12 weeks is far past neurulation.
- Vitamin A in high doses (>10,000 IU) is highly teratogenic (causes craniofacial and cardiac defects).
- Pyridoxine does not prevent neural tube defects.

question: A 22-year-old unimmunized woman with no prenatal care presents in labor at 36 weeks gestation. Ultrasound reveals polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index 28 cm). Delivery produces a stillborn infant with complete absence of the calvarium, scalp, and cerebral hemispheres, but the brainstem is partially preserved. The fetal eyes bulge prominently, giving a 'frog-like' appearance. What is the diagnosis, and what explains the polyhydramnios?

options.text: Anencephaly; polyhydramnios results from impaired fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid due to lack of forebrain swallowing centers
Holoprosencephaly; polyhydramnios results from esophageal atresia
Encephalocele; polyhydramnios results from renal agenesis
Chiari II malformation; polyhydramnios results from duodenal web
Hydranencephaly; polyhydramnios results from lack of fetal urination

explanation:
Anencephaly (meroencephaly) is a lethal congenital malformation resulting from failure of the anterior (rostral) neuropore to close on embryonic day 25. The neurocranium (calvarium) fails to form, exposing the developing brain tissue to amniotic fluid, which leads to necrosis and degeneration of the cerebral hemispheres. The brainstem may be preserved. Polyhydramnios develops because fetal swallowing of amniotic fluid (normally regulated by forebrain and diencephalic centers) is absent, so fluid accumulates in the amniotic cavity.

Distractor rationales:
- Holoprosencephaly features fused hemispheres, not absent calvarium and forebrain.
- Encephalocele is a localized skull defect with herniation.
- Hydranencephaly is liquefaction of cerebral hemispheres due to massive bilateral ICA occlusion in utero; the calvarium and scalp are intact.
- Polyhydramnios is caused by impaired swallowing, not duodenal web in this setting.

question: A newborn is noted to have a 4 cm skin-covered sac protruding from the occipital region of the skull through a bony defect (cranium bifidum). Biopsy of the sac wall shows meninges and disorganized cerebral cortex tissue. What is this malformation, and which syndromic triad should be considered if polycystic kidneys and polydactyly are also present?

options.text: Encephalocele; Meckel-Gruber syndrome
Anencephaly; Edwards syndrome
Meningocele; Patau syndrome
Craniosynostosis; Apert syndrome
Holoprosencephaly; Down syndrome

explanation:
An encephalocele (meningoencephalocele) is a neural tube defect characterized by herniation of intracranial contents (meninges and brain parenchyma) through a defect in the skull (cranium bifidum), most commonly occurring in the occipital region. When associated with the classic triad of occipital encephalocele, bilateral dysplastic polycystic kidneys, and postaxial polydactyly, it is diagnostic of MECKEL-GRUBER SYNDROME (an autosomal recessive ciliopathy lethal in infancy).

Distractor rationales:
- Anencephaly is complete absence of forebrain and calvarium.
- Meningocele involves herniation of meninges only, without brain tissue.
- Apert syndrome is craniosynostosis with severe syndactyly (FGFR2 mutation).
- Holoprosencephaly is failed hemispheric cleavage.
